stages.title: Template
stages.text: Follow the DNA template. RNA polymerase binds at the promoter and builds a complementary messenger RNA strand.

stages.title: Message
stages.text: Watch the RNA message lengthen and leave the template. This is transcription. The DNA sequence provides the information; the RNA carries a copy.

stages.title: Next step
stages.text: Translation comes next at a ribosome. Transfer RNA matches messenger codons while a polypeptide is assembled. Do not confuse message production with protein assembly.

stages.title: Insulin resistance
stages.text: Chapter five. Obesity is a risk factor for type two diabetes, but the connection is more than a label. The supplied notes describe insulin resistance: cells have difficulty using the insulin present.

stages.title: Supply contrast
stages.text: Watch the tissue response weaken while insulin remains available. Contrast this with type one diabetes, where autoimmune destruction reduces the pancreatic beta-cell supply.

stages.title: Modifiable risk
stages.text: Family history also changes risk. Exercise and weight management address modifiable contributors; they do not erase inherited susceptibility.

stages.title: Chromatin
stages.text: DNA wraps around histone proteins. Tight packing is heterochromatin; loose packing is euchromatin.

stages.title: Silencing
stages.text: Now add methyl groups at a promoter. The supplied cancer example links heavy promoter methylation with reduced tumor-suppressor transcription. The base sequence need not change.

stages.title: Different outcomes
stages.text: A chemical modification can change gene activity. Different expression patterns help cells acquire different identities, even when they carry the same DNA.

stages.title: Boundary
stages.text: A tumor can enlarge without yet establishing a distant deposit. First examine its boundary with surrounding tissue.

stages.title: Invasion
stages.text: Watch protease activity open a path through extracellular matrix and basement membrane. Reduced adhesion and increased migration help cells leave the original site.

stages.title: Metastasis
stages.text: Entry into blood or lymph is not enough. Cells must survive transport and grow in a receptive distant environment. Local invasion and successful metastasis are separate steps.

stages.title: Active tissue
stages.text: Adipose tissue is an active participant in the cancer-risk model. It releases adipokines.

stages.title: Interacting pathways
stages.text: With obesity, the supplied deck links insulin resistance and hyperinsulinemia. Watch signaling increase around the tissue. This is a risk mechanism, not proof that a tumor will develop.

stages.title: Activity
stages.text: Physical activity can reduce inflammatory mediators and insulin-like growth factors. The packet describes protection for selected cancers even without weight loss.

stages.title: Development
stages.text: Childhood cancer is not simply adult cancer occurring earlier. The supplied chapter emphasizes immature tissues and developmental origins.

stages.title: Diverging states
stages.text: Compare two paths. In one, immature cells mature and differentiate. In the embryonal-tumor model, tissue fails to differentiate and retains an immature pattern.

stages.title: Scope
stages.text: Many childhood cancers arise from mesodermal tissues. Growth timing, inherited factors and exposures belong to the same assessment; no single factor explains every case.

stages.title: Compression
stages.text: Pressure over a bony prominence can compress the local capillary bed. Watch flow diminish as the tissue is compressed.

stages.title: Ischemia
stages.text: Unrelieved pressure reduces oxygen delivery and can cause ischemia and necrosis. Depth matters: injury can extend from skin into deeper supporting tissues.

stages.title: Relief
stages.text: Pressure relief and repositioning address the initiating force. An intact red surface and an exposed deep wound represent different findings; a covered wound base may prevent staging.

stages.title: Barrier
stages.text: Atopic dermatitis involves epidermal barrier dysfunction and immune dysregulation. Filaggrin alteration is one supplied barrier mechanism.

stages.title: Scratching
stages.text: Severe itching drives scratching. Watch the surface become disrupted, followed by a thickened epidermis with repeated scratching. The thickening is lichenification.

stages.title: Care
stages.text: Hydration and emollients support barrier care. Distribution changes with age: infants often have face and extensor lesions, while older children favor flexures.

stages.title: Leak
stages.text: After a major burn, fluid shifts out of the circulation and tissue edema develops. Watch fluid collect outside the vessel while the circulating supply falls.

stages.title: Replacement
stages.text: Visible swelling does not prove adequate blood volume. Fluid replacement supports the circulation; increasing capillary permeability is not its purpose.

stages.title: Monitoring
stages.text: The supplied deck identifies urine output as the most reliable resuscitation measure. Capillary seal marks the end of burn shock in this source.

stages.title: Early shock
stages.text: A child can have poor tissue perfusion while systolic pressure remains appropriate for age. This is compensated shock.

stages.title: Redistribution
stages.text: Watch peripheral flow decrease as blood is redistributed. A normal pressure reading does not erase abnormal perfusion findings.

stages.title: Deterioration
stages.text: Hypotension marks a later category. Bradycardia in a severely ill child can signal deterioration, and hypoxia is a common cause. Assess oxygen delivery and perfusion together.
